title: Environment and Resources
overview: Say what will be going on at a future moment, not just what will happen. Describe a trend without claiming the movement stopped when the record did. Carry a cause through four steps in one sentence, and then test every link. Above all, keep a correlation from turning into a cause on its way through your writing.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account by somebody who prepares figures, a page about reading data, and a monitoring summary.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Say what you will be doing at a given point next year
Describe a trend without overstating where it stopped
Write about a future figure and say what it depends on
Explain how one thing led to another, through several steps
Tell whether a report has shown a cause or found a pattern
Present figures without claiming more than they show
Say what is scarce, finite or abundant, and mean different things
lectureScript:
This unit is about figures, and about the very small changes in wording that decide whether a figure is honestly reported.
The grammar in it is the last verb form in the course, and the rest is about restraint.

The new form first. The future continuous.
Will, be, and an -ing form. This time next year we will be using the new system.
It describes something that will already be GOING ON at a point in the future, rather than something that happens then.
Compare these two, because they are different claims.
We will use the new system in March means March is when it starts.
We will be using it in March means it will already be running.
It has a second use that is worth having in conversation.
Will you be coming to the meeting asks about your plans. Will you come asks you to commit.
The continuous one is politer, and that is why.
The error is always the same. Do not drop the be. Will is followed by a plain verb, and here the plain verb is be.

The second card takes a form you already own and puts it to work on data.
You have used the past continuous for a long stretch, for a background and for two things running together.
Here it describes a figure that was moving, and a measurement that was being taken.
Emissions were rising steadily until 2019. Only two pollutants were being measured at that time.
Put those two together and you have a methods section: the trend is real, and the data was partial.
Now the part that matters most, and the reading in this unit is built round it.
Somebody who prepares water figures says they cannot write emissions rose until 2019.
Their series ends in 2019 because the station was moved. The movement did not stop. The record did.
Emissions rose until 2019 claims a finished movement. Emissions were rising until 2019 says only what they know.
One word, and it is the difference between accurate and not.

The third card is about writing a figure for a year that has not arrived.
Is expected to. Is projected to. Is forecast to. Is likely to. Is due to. Is set to.
All of them take to and a plain verb, and all of them are passive, which means none of them says who is doing the expecting.
That is the by-whom question from Unit 4 arriving somewhere new, and it is worth asking every time.
And every projection rests on an assumption, whether it states one or not.
Consumption is projected to fall by 2030, assuming rainfall stays at the recent average.
Without those last words it is not a finding. It is a sentence.

The fourth card gives you something none of the earlier connective work could.
Units 6, 7 and 13 gave you contrast, reason, purpose and conclusion. None of them carries a cause through several steps.
Which in turn does, and it takes a full verb. Warmer water holds less oxygen, which in turn reduces fish numbers.
Thereby does too, and it takes an -ing form. The store was enlarged, thereby reducing pressure on the aquifer.
You can run four steps through a single sentence, and reports do.
But here is the thing to keep. Every link is a separate claim.
A four-step chain makes four assertions, and a reader may accept three and reject the fourth.

Which brings us to the last card, and it is the one I would keep if I could keep only one from this level.
When two things move together, there are exactly four possibilities.
A causes B. B causes A. Something else causes both. Or coincidence.
A chart cannot tell you which, and the third is the commonest.
There is an old example. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July, and nobody thinks ice cream causes drowning, because the third factor is obvious.
In real work it is almost never obvious.
So there is one test, and it is short. Before you write that X causes Y, ask whether you can say HOW.
If you can describe a mechanism, you may have a cause. If you cannot, you have a correlation, and there is a perfectly good word for it.
And watch the subtle version, because it is the one that catches careful people.
It is rarely a flat claim. It is a chain. X rose, which in turn lowered Y.
That which in turn has just asserted a mechanism, and the phrase did it rather than the writer.
One last thing from the reading, which I think is true of a great deal of writing and not only about data.
The hedges are the first thing removed when a sentence travels. By the time it reaches a summary, were rising has become rose, and after has become because.
Neither change was dishonest. Both were somebody making a sentence shorter.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: Able to be replaced naturally as it is used.
words.example: About a third of the supply is now renewable.
practice: Renewable means the source refills itself.
It is the opposite of finite in this context.
Its verb is renew, and its noun renewal.
Renewables, as a plural noun, means the sources themselves.
words.starter: About … of the supply is renewable.
words.tutor: Describe a renewable source. Ask the tutor what makes it renewable.

words.meaning: Having a limit; there is only so much of it.
words.example: Fresh water is finite in any one place.
practice: Finite means there is an end to it.
Its opposite is infinite, with in-.
It is pronounced FY-nite.
Finite is about the total, not about the speed of use.
words.tutor: Describe something finite. Ask the tutor whether it is about total or speed.

words.meaning: Not available in enough quantity.
words.example: Skilled labour is scarce in the region.
practice: Scarce is about availability now, not about the total.
Its noun is scarcity.
Scarcely, the adverb, means hardly, which is a different idea.
Something finite need not be scarce yet.
words.tutor: Describe something scarce. Ask the tutor how it differs from finite.

words.meaning: Present in large quantities.
words.example: Wind is abundant here and difficult to store.
practice: Abundant is the opposite of scarce.
Its noun is abundance.
Abundant takes in for where: abundant in the north.
Abundance does not mean easy to use.
words.tutor: Describe something abundant. Ask the tutor whether abundant means useful.

words.meaning: The amount of something used up.
words.example: Consumption fell by four per cent over the decade.
practice: Consumption takes of.
Its verb is consume.
Consumption measures use; production measures supply.
Per capita consumption is consumption divided by population.
words.tutor: State a consumption figure. Ask the tutor whether you gave a period.

words.meaning: The reduction of a supply by use.
words.example: Depletion of the aquifer has accelerated since 2015.
practice: Depletion takes of.
Its verb is deplete.
Depletion is the process; scarcity is the result.
A depleted resource may still have some left.
words.tutor: Describe depletion. Ask the tutor how it differs from scarcity.

words.meaning: Gases or particles released into the air.
words.example: Emissions were rising steadily until 2019.
practice: Emissions is almost always plural.
Its verb is emit, which doubles the t: emitted.
Emissions takes from for the source.
It takes a plural verb: emissions were rising.
words.tutor: Describe emissions. Ask the tutor to check the verb agreed.

words.meaning: A substance that causes pollution.
words.example: Three pollutants are measured at each station.
practice: A pollutant is the substance; pollution is the condition.
Its verb is pollute.
-ant names a thing or a person that does something.
A pollutant is only a pollutant where it does not belong.
words.tutor: Name a pollutant. Ask the tutor how it differs from pollution.

words.meaning: The natural home of a plant or animal.
words.example: The habitat was being surveyed when the work stopped.
practice: A habitat is where something lives.
It takes for: a habitat for wading birds.
Habitat loss is the commonest phrase.
It is pronounced HAB-i-tat.
words.tutor: Describe a habitat. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: The variety of living things in a place.
words.example: Biodiversity has declined across all four sites.
practice: Bio- means life; diversity means variety.
Biodiversity is uncountable.
It counts variety, not quantity.
A place can have many animals and low biodiversity.
words.tutor: Describe biodiversity. Ask the tutor what it actually counts.

words.meaning: A community of living things and the place they live in.
words.example: The whole ecosystem depends on the water level.
practice: An ecosystem includes the living and the non-living together.
It is one word.
A habitat is a home; an ecosystem is a system.
The stress is on the first part: EE-co-system.
words.tutor: Describe an ecosystem. Ask the tutor how it differs from a habitat.

words.meaning: The presence of something harmful where it should not be.
words.example: Contamination was detected at two of the wells.
practice: Contamination takes of, and by for the substance.
Its verb is contaminate.
Contamination is local; pollution is usually broader.
It is often found in the passive: was contaminated.
words.tutor: Report contamination. Ask the tutor to check the prepositions.

words.meaning: To be one of several causes of something.
words.example: Transport contributes about a quarter of the total.
practice: Contribute takes to.
It says one of several, which is honest and useful.
Its noun is contribution.
Contributing is weaker than causing, deliberately.
words.tutor: Say what contributes to something. Ask the tutor why it is weaker than causes.

words.meaning: To make something happen faster.
words.example: Depletion has accelerated since 2015.
practice: Accelerate can take an object or none.
Its noun is acceleration.
Accelerating is about the rate, not the amount.
Something can accelerate while the total still falls.
words.tutor: Describe an acceleration. Ask the tutor whether the total also rose.

words.meaning: To balance one effect with an opposite one.
words.example: The gain was offset by higher consumption elsewhere.
practice: Offset takes by for the balancing thing.
Its past forms are offset and offset: it never changes.
Offsetting cancels; it does not remove.
It is also a noun: a carbon offset.
words.tutor: Describe an offset. Ask the tutor whether it removed the problem.

words.meaning: To make a bad situation worse.
words.example: The dry summer exacerbated the shortage.
practice: Exacerbate takes a direct object.
It applies only to things that are already bad.
Its noun is exacerbation.
It is pronounced ig-ZAS-er-bate.
words.tutor: Describe something exacerbating a problem. Ask the tutor to check the stress.

words.meaning: To make a bad situation less severe.
words.example: The new store alleviated the shortage but did not end it.
practice: Alleviate is the opposite of exacerbate.
It takes a direct object.
Alleviating reduces; solving removes.
Its noun is alleviation.
words.tutor: Describe alleviation. Ask the tutor how it differs from solving.

words.meaning: To act against something so as to reduce its effect.
words.example: Nothing was done to counteract the rise.
practice: Counter- means against.
Counteract takes a direct object.
Counteracting is deliberate; offsetting may be accidental.
It is one word.
words.tutor: Describe counteracting something. Ask the tutor how it differs from offsetting.

words.meaning: The level at which something changes or becomes serious.
words.example: Two readings were above the threshold.
practice: A threshold is a limit with a consequence attached.
It takes for: the threshold for action.
It also means a doorway.
Crossing a threshold triggers something; a target does not.
words.starter: … readings were above the threshold for …
words.tutor: Describe a threshold. Ask the tutor what it triggers.

words.meaning: The starting measurement everything else is compared with.
words.example: The 2010 figure is used as the baseline.
practice: A baseline is a reference point, chosen deliberately.
Changing the baseline changes every comparison.
It is one word.
Always ask what baseline a percentage is against.
words.starter: The … figure is used as the baseline.
words.tutor: Name a baseline. Ask the tutor what changing it would do.

words.meaning: The general direction of change over time.
words.example: The trend is downward, with two bad years in it.
practice: A trend is a direction, not a single measurement.
It takes in: a trend in consumption.
Two points do not make a trend.
Its adjective is trending, which is recent.
words.tutor: Describe a trend. Ask the tutor how many points make one.

words.meaning: A relationship in which two things change together.
words.example: There is a strong correlation between the two.
practice: Correlation takes between, or with.
It says they move together, not that one causes the other.
Its verb is correlate.
This distinction is the subject of a whole card in this unit.
words.starter: There is a correlation between … and …
words.tutor: Describe a correlation. Ask the tutor what it does NOT show.

words.meaning: An estimate of a future figure, based on present data.
words.example: The projection assumes consumption stays flat.
practice: A projection is not a prediction: it carries assumptions.
Its verb is project, stressed pro-JECT.
Every projection depends on what it assumed.
Ask what the assumptions are, always.
words.tutor: Describe a projection. Ask the tutor what question it invites.

words.meaning: A measurement used to show how something is changing.
words.example: Water level is the best single indicator we have.
practice: An indicator stands for something harder to measure.
It takes of, or for.
Its verb is indicate, from Unit 4.
A good indicator moves when the real thing moves.
words.tutor: Name an indicator. Ask the tutor what it stands for.

words.meaning: To seem to be the case, on the evidence available.
words.example: Emissions appear to have peaked in 2019.
practice: Appear takes to plus a plain verb.
It hedges without weakening you unfairly.
It is a state verb: no continuous form here.
It also means to become visible, which is different.
words.tutor: Hedge a claim with appear. Ask the tutor to check the form after it.

words.meaning: To calculate an approximate figure.
words.example: Consumption is estimated at forty thousand litres.
practice: Estimate takes at for the figure.
It is also a noun, said differently: ES-ti-mut.
An estimate should carry a range or a margin.
Estimated is very common in the passive.
words.tutor: State an estimate. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: About; close to but not exactly.
words.example: Approximately a third of the supply is renewable.
practice: Approximately is the formal about.
It should not sit in front of a precise figure.
Approximately 40,000 is fine; approximately 41,237 is not.
Its adjective is approximate.
words.tutor: State an approximate figure. Ask the tutor whether it was too precise.

words.meaning: In general terms, with exceptions allowed for.
words.example: The trend is broadly downward.
practice: Broadly admits exceptions without listing them.
Broadly speaking is the fixed phrase.
It is honest hedging: it says the detail is untidy.
Its adjective is broad.
words.tutor: Hedge a trend with broadly. Ask the tutor what it admits.

words.meaning: Not final; offered subject to change.
words.example: These are tentative figures and may be revised.
practice: Tentative means provisional and says so.
Its adverb is tentatively.
A tentative conclusion invites challenge, which is its purpose.
It is stronger than a guess and weaker than a finding.
words.tutor: Label something tentative. Ask the tutor what it invites.

grammar.title: This time next year: already under way
grammar.explanation:
This is the last verb form in the course, and it is new.
It describes something that will be in progress at a stated point in the
future, rather than something that will simply happen.
Reports and plans use it constantly, because a plan is a description of what
will be going on.
grammar.rule:
will + BE + the -ing form

This time next year we will be using the new system.
By March they will be operating from two sites.
The station will be measuring three pollutants from April.

Compare the two, because they are different claims:
We will use the new system in March.        (it starts then)
We will be using it in March.               (it will already be running)

IT ALSO REMOVES INTENTION, which is why it is useful in conversation:
Will you be coming to the meeting?
That asks about your plans. Will you come? asks you to commit.
The continuous version is the politer of the two for that reason.

THE PASSIVE exists and is rarer:
The site will be being surveyed. — correct, and almost nobody writes it.
Prefer: the survey will be under way.

And the usual rule holds: state verbs stay simple. Not I will be knowing.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Say that the new system is already running by the time March arrives.
1. Is this a starting point, or a state of affairs at a moment?
2. A state of affairs at a moment, so the continuous.
3. will + be + the -ing form.
Answer: By March we will be using the new system.
We will use it in March would mean March is when it starts.
grammar.mistake:
The be is what gets dropped, exactly as in the passive.
No: This time next year we will using it.
Yes: This time next year we will be using it.
will is always followed by a plain verb, and here the plain verb is be.
grammar.tip: will be + -ing = it will already be going on. It also asks about plans without demanding a commitment.
grammar.practice:
Write the future continuous.
1. The new system ___ (run) by this time next year.
2. By March they ___ (operate) from two sites.
3. The station ___ (measure) three pollutants from April.
Now choose the better form and say why.
4. We (will use / will be using) the new system in March. (it starts then)
5. We (will use / will be using) it in March. (it is already running)
6. (Will you come / Will you be coming) to the meeting? (you want their plans,
   not a commitment)
Now correct this.
7. This time next year we will using the new system.
grammar.answers:
1. will be running  2. will be operating  3. will be measuring
4. will use (March is when it begins)
5. will be using (it is already under way)
6. Will you be coming (it asks about plans rather than asking them to commit)
7. will BE using.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Emissions were rising: a measurement that was moving
grammar.explanation:
You have used the past continuous for a long stretch, for a background, and
for two things running together. It has one more job, and a report depends
on it: describing a FIGURE that was moving over a stated period.
grammar.rule:
ACTIVE — the figure moves:
Emissions were rising steadily until 2019.
Consumption was falling in the north and rising in the south.
Numbers were recovering before the second dry summer.

PASSIVE — the figure was being taken:
Only two pollutants were being measured at that time.
The habitat was being surveyed when the work stopped.
Water levels were not being recorded before 2015.

The pair together is what a methods section is made of:
Emissions were rising, but only two pollutants were being measured.
That sentence says the trend is real AND the data was partial.

AGAINST THE PAST SIMPLE:
Emissions rose in 2019.          one finished movement
Emissions were rising in 2019.   it was under way, and continued

AND THE HONEST USE: the continuous admits the period was not complete.
If the series stops mid-trend, were rising is accurate and rose is not.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The figures stop in 2019 and the line is still going up. How do you write it?
1. Did the movement finish? No — the data finished.
2. The past simple would say it rose and stopped.
3. The continuous says it was under way when the record ends.
Answer: Emissions were rising until 2019, when the series ends.
Emissions rose until 2019 claims something the data does not support.
grammar.mistake:
Using the past simple for an incomplete series overstates what you know.
Emissions rose until 2019 suggests a movement that finished in 2019.
Emissions were rising until 2019 says only that the record stops there.
In a report that difference is the difference between accurate and not.
grammar.tip: The continuous says it was under way. The simple says it finished.
grammar.practice:
Choose the past simple or the past continuous.
1. Emissions ___ (rise) steadily until 2019, where the data ends.
2. Emissions ___ (rise) by four per cent in 2019.
3. Only two pollutants ___ (measure, passive) at that time.
4. The habitat ___ (survey, passive) when the work stopped.
5. Water levels ___ (not record, passive) before 2015.
6. Consumption ___ (fall) in the north and ___ (rise) in the south.
Now write one sentence saying the trend was real and the data was partial.
grammar.answers:
1. were rising  2. rose  3. were being measured  4. was being surveyed
5. were not being recorded  6. was falling / rising
7. Emissions were rising, but only two pollutants were being measured.
Numbers 1 and 2 are the pair: an unfinished record against a finished year.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Is projected to rise: writing about what has not happened
grammar.explanation:
Unit 5 chose a future form by the evidence behind it. Unit 10 built the
future passive. This card is the register those two lead to: how a report
states a figure for a year that has not arrived.
Every one of these forms carries an assumption, and the skill is seeing it.
grammar.rule:
IS EXPECTED TO      widely anticipated, source unstated
  Consumption is expected to fall by 2030.
IS PROJECTED TO     calculated from present data
  Depletion is projected to accelerate.
IS FORECAST TO      calculated, usually short term
IS LIKELY TO        probable, and hedged
IS DUE TO           scheduled, by a plan or a timetable
IS SET TO           arranged, and close to certain

All of them take TO plus a plain verb, and all are passive, so none names
who expects, projects or forecasts. That is the question to ask.

AND THE ASSUMPTION IS ALWAYS THERE, stated or not:
The projection assumes consumption stays flat.
On current trends, the threshold will be crossed by 2040.
If nothing changes, emissions will be rising again by 2035.

A projection without its assumption is not a finding. It is a sentence.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You have a calculation showing depletion getting faster. Write it.
1. Is it widely anticipated, or calculated from data? Calculated.
2. Calculated from present data is projected.
3. It takes to plus a plain verb.
4. And it needs its assumption, or a reader cannot weigh it.
Answer: Depletion is projected to accelerate, assuming consumption stays flat.
Without the last four words the sentence claims more than the calculation does.
grammar.mistake:
These forms are all passive, so they never say who is doing the projecting.
Emissions are expected to fall — expected by whom, and on what basis?
It is the by whom question from Unit 4, arriving in a new place.
grammar.tip: Every projection rests on an assumption. State it, or ask for it.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form.
1. A calculation from present data shows depletion getting faster. ___
2. A timetable says the station opens in April. ___
3. It is probable but not certain that consumption will fall. ___
4. Everybody anticipates a fall, though nobody is named. ___
Now add the missing assumption to each.
5. Consumption is projected to fall by 2030.
6. The threshold will be crossed by 2040.
Now answer.
7. What question does every one of these forms leave unanswered?
grammar.answers:
1. is projected to accelerate  2. is due to open  3. is likely to fall
4. is expected to fall
5. ... assuming the new store remains in use. (any stated assumption)
6. On current trends, the threshold will be crossed by 2040.
7. By whom? All of them are passive, so none names who is projecting.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Which in turn: following a cause down the chain
grammar.explanation:
Units 6, 7 and 13 gave you connectives for contrast, reason, purpose and
conclusion. None of them can do the thing an environmental argument needs
most: carry a cause through three or four steps without starting a new
sentence each time.
grammar.rule:
WHICH IN TURN — the effect becomes the next cause:
Warmer water holds less oxygen, which in turn reduces fish numbers.

THEREBY + -ING — the same action produces this as well:
The store was enlarged, thereby reducing pressure on the aquifer.
Note the -ing: thereby reducing, never thereby reduces.

THUS LEADING TO / RESULTING IN — a further consequence:
Rainfall fell, resulting in lower recharge and a longer dry season.

A FULL CHAIN, four steps in one sentence:
Consumption rose faster than recharge, depleting the aquifer, which in turn
lowered the water table, thereby drying out the habitat downstream.

WORTH KNOWING: each link is a claim, and a chain is only as strong as its
weakest link. A reader may accept three and reject the fourth.
So the longer the chain, the more useful a hedge inside it:
... which in turn appears to have lowered the water table.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these into one chain: consumption rose; the aquifer was depleted; the
water table fell; the habitat dried out.
1. Start with the first cause: consumption rose faster than recharge.
2. The next step is caused by it, so use an -ing form: depleting the aquifer.
3. The third step follows from the second: which in turn lowered the water table.
4. The fourth follows from the third: thereby drying out the habitat.
Answer: the four-step sentence above.
Read it back and count the claims. There are four, and each can be argued with.
grammar.mistake:
thereby takes an -ing form, and learners write a finite verb after it.
No: The store was enlarged, thereby reduced pressure on the aquifer.
Yes: ... thereby reducing pressure on the aquifer.
which in turn is the one that takes a full verb: which in turn reduced it.
grammar.tip: which in turn takes a verb. thereby takes -ing. Every link is a separate claim.
grammar.practice:
Join each set into one chain.
1. Warmer water holds less oxygen. Fish numbers fall. (which in turn)
2. The store was enlarged. Pressure on the aquifer fell. (thereby)
3. Rainfall fell. Recharge was lower. The dry season was longer. (resulting in)
4. Consumption rose. The aquifer was depleted. The water table fell.
   The habitat dried out. (make one four-step chain)
Now correct this.
5. The store was enlarged, thereby reduced pressure on the aquifer.
Now answer.
6. How many separate claims does your answer to 4 contain?
grammar.answers:
1. Warmer water holds less oxygen, which in turn reduces fish numbers.
2. The store was enlarged, thereby reducing pressure on the aquifer.
3. Rainfall fell, resulting in lower recharge and a longer dry season.
4. Consumption rose faster than recharge, depleting the aquifer, which in turn
   lowered the water table, thereby drying out the habitat downstream.
5. thereby REDUCING.
6. Four. A reader may accept three and reject the fourth.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Correlation is not cause
grammar.explanation:
This is the last card in the level that is about honesty rather than form,
and it is the one most worth keeping.
Two things that move together may be connected in four different ways, and
English has separate language for each. Using the wrong one claims more than
you know.
grammar.rule:
THE FOUR POSSIBILITIES, whenever two things move together:
1. A causes B.
2. B causes A.
3. Something else causes both.
4. Coincidence.
A correlation on its own does not tell you which.

THE LANGUAGE OF CORRELATION — safe, and says only what you saw:
There is a strong correlation between the two.
The two move together.
X is associated with Y.
Where X rises, Y tends to fall.

THE LANGUAGE OF CAUSE — claims a mechanism:
X causes Y.  X leads to Y.  X drives Y.  X is responsible for Y.

AND THE HONEST MIDDLE, which is where most real writing sits:
X contributes to Y.        (one of several causes)
X appears to have caused Y. (a cause, hedged)
X may account for part of Y.

The test before you write causes: can you say HOW? If you cannot describe
the mechanism, you have a correlation and you should say so.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in July. Write it honestly.
1. Do they move together? Yes.
2. Can you describe a mechanism from one to the other? No.
3. Is there a plausible third cause? Yes: hot weather.
Answer: Ice cream sales and drownings are correlated, though both are
probably driven by warm weather.
Writing ice cream causes drowning is the same data and a false claim.
grammar.mistake:
The commonest failure is not claiming cause outright. It is a chain that
quietly turns a correlation into one.
Emissions rose and biodiversity fell, which in turn ...
That which in turn has just asserted a mechanism you may not have.
Check every link of a chain against the same test: can you say how?
grammar.tip: Can you say HOW? If not, you have a correlation, and the word for it is correlation.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one at the strength the evidence supports.
1. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July, so ice cream causes drowning.
2. Emissions rose and biodiversity fell, so emissions destroyed the habitat.
3. Transport is about a quarter of the total, so transport causes the problem.
4. Depletion accelerated after 2015 and the new well opened in 2015.
Now answer.
5. Name the four ways two things that move together may be related.
6. What is the test before writing causes?
grammar.answers:
1. They are correlated, and both are probably driven by warm weather.
2. Emissions rose and biodiversity fell over the same period. Any causal link
   would need a mechanism, which these figures do not give.
3. Transport contributes about a quarter of the total.
4. Depletion accelerated after the well opened, though the figures alone do
   not establish that the well caused it.
5. A causes B; B causes A; something else causes both; coincidence.
6. Can you say HOW? If not, it is a correlation.
5 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Year the Data Stopped
readings.setting: Told by somebody who prepares figures
readings.passage:
I prepare the water figures for four sites and I have learned to be careful about two words.
The first is rose. Our series ends in 2019 because the station was moved and the readings are not comparable after that.
So emissions rose until 2019 is not something I can write. The movement did not stop in 2019. The record did.
What I write is emissions were rising until 2019, which says only what I know.
The second word is caused.
Depletion accelerated after 2015 and a new well opened in 2015, and those two facts sit next to each other on every chart I produce.
Somebody asks me every year whether the well caused it, and the honest answer is that I cannot tell from these numbers.
It might have. Consumption might have risen anyway. Rainfall was also lower from 2016.
So I write that depletion accelerated after the well opened, and I put the rainfall series on the same page.
Granted, that is less useful than an answer. It is also the only thing the data supports.
What I have noticed is that the hedges are the first thing removed when a figure travels.
By the time my sentence reaches a summary, were rising has become rose and after has become because.
Neither change was dishonest. Both were somebody making a sentence shorter.

readings.title: Four Ways Two Things Move Together
readings.passage:
When two measurements rise and fall together, there are exactly four possibilities, and no chart can tell you which.
The first is that one causes the other.
The second is that the other causes the first, which is easier to overlook than it sounds.
The third is that something else causes both, and this is the commonest of the four.
The fourth is coincidence, which is rarer than people think but not impossible.
There is an old example. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July.
Nobody believes ice cream causes drowning, because we can all see the third factor: hot weather.
The example is useful precisely because the third factor is obvious. In real work it rarely is.
There is one test that does most of the job.
Before you write that X causes Y, ask whether you can describe HOW.
If you can name a mechanism, you may have a cause. If you cannot, you have a correlation, and there is a perfectly good word for that.
The subtle failure is not claiming cause outright. It is the chain.
Writing X rose, which in turn lowered Y quietly asserts a mechanism, and the phrase which in turn is doing it rather than the writer.
Check every link in a chain against the same question.

readings.title: Monitoring Summary: Aquifer, Sites 1 to 4
readings.passage:
AQUIFER MONITORING SUMMARY
Period: 2010 to 2024        Baseline: 2010

1. Data
Water levels were being recorded at all four sites from 2010.
Only two pollutants were being measured before 2015; four are measured now.
The 2019 series ends at site 3, where the station was relocated.

2. Trend
Consumption was rising steadily until 2019. It appears to have levelled since.
Depletion accelerated after 2015. A new well opened in the same year, and
rainfall was also lower from 2016. These figures do not establish which, if either,
is responsible.

3. Thresholds
Two readings at site 2 were above the threshold for contamination.
Biodiversity indicators are broadly unchanged, with one site declining.

4. Projection
On current trends, consumption is projected to exceed recharge by 2031.
This projection assumes rainfall remains at the 2016 to 2024 average.
By 2031 the site will be operating under the revised abstraction limit.

5. Note
Figures for site 3 after 2019 are tentative and may be revised.

comprehension.q: Why can the writer not say 'emissions rose until 2019'?
comprehension.a: The movement did not stop in 2019; the record did, because the station was moved.
comprehension.why: The past simple would claim a finished movement the data does not show.

comprehension.q: Why will the writer not say the new well caused the depletion?
comprehension.a: Consumption might have risen anyway, and rainfall was also lower from 2016.
comprehension.why: Two other explanations are live, so the figures do not settle it.

comprehension.q: What happens to the hedges when a figure travels?
comprehension.a: They are removed: 'were rising' becomes 'rose' and 'after' becomes 'because'.
comprehension.why: The writer says neither change was dishonest; both were somebody shortening a sentence.

comprehension.q: What does the writer put on the same page as the depletion figures, and why?
comprehension.a: The rainfall series, because it is a rival explanation.
comprehension.why: Showing it lets the reader weigh the third possibility themselves.

comprehension.q: What are the four possibilities when two measurements move together?
comprehension.a: A causes B; B causes A; something else causes both; coincidence.
comprehension.why: Listed in order, with the third called the commonest.

comprehension.q: Why is the ice cream example useful?
comprehension.a: Because the third factor, hot weather, is obvious. In real work it rarely is.
comprehension.why: The article says that is precisely why it is a good teaching example and a poor model.

comprehension.q: What does the article call the subtle failure?
comprehension.a: A causal chain, where 'which in turn' asserts a mechanism the writer has not shown.
comprehension.why: The phrase does the claiming rather than the writer, which is why it slips past.

comprehension.q: How many pollutants were measured before 2015, and how many now?
comprehension.why: Section 1, in the past continuous passive, which marks it as the arrangement at that time.

comprehension.a: That rainfall remains at the 2016 to 2024 average.
comprehension.why: Section 4 states the assumption, which is what makes it a finding rather than a sentence.

comprehension.q: Section 2 says the figures 'do not establish which, if either, is responsible'. What is it refusing to do?
comprehension.a: Turn a correlation into a cause.
comprehension.why: Two events share a year, and the summary declines to claim a mechanism it cannot show.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — This time next year
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences about your own life or work a year from now.
Every one must use will be plus an -ing form.
Models:
This time next year I will be working in a different department.
By March we will be using the new system.
I will be finishing the course about this time next year.
Now say six of your own. Invented is fine.
Tap the mic. Say all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: did every one contain the word be?
Does each one describe something already GOING ON at that moment,
rather than something that starts then?
speaking.tutor: Say your six and ask the tutor whether any of them described a starting point instead.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Three weak words before the main one
speaking.instructions:
The future continuous and the continuous passive both stack small unstressed
words in front of the main word. Learners produce only the last.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
we will be USing       sounds like  we-l-bee-USing
they will be oPERating sounds like  they-l-bee-oPERating
were being MEASured    sounds like  wuh-bee-in MEASured
was being surVEYED     sounds like  wuz-bee-in surVEYED
The respelling is a hint for your ear. Always write will be, were being.
Now say these three lines.
This time next year we will be using the new system.
Only two pollutants were being measured at that time.
By 2031 the site will be operating under the revised limit.
Tap the mic. Say the three lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: is the be there in every one, quick and quiet?
speaking.tutor: Say the three lines and ask the tutor whether any be or being went missing.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say only what the data shows
speaking.instructions:
For each situation, say aloud the sentence the evidence actually supports.
1. The series ends in 2019 and the line is still going up.
2. Only two pollutants were measured before 2015.
3. Depletion got faster after 2015; a well opened in 2015; rainfall also fell.
4. Transport is about a quarter of the total.
5. Two readings were over the limit; the rest were not.
Models:
Emissions were rising until 2019, where the series ends.
Transport contributes about a quarter of the total.
Tap the mic. Say all five. Tap again and listen.
Check: in number 3, did you say caused? You should not have.
In number 4, did you say causes? Contributes is the honest word.
speaking.tutor: Say your five and ask the tutor which one claimed more than the evidence allowed.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the year the data stopped
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
I prepare the water figures for four sites and I am careful about two words.
The first is rose. Our series ends in 2019 because the station was moved.
So emissions rose until 2019 is not something I can write. The movement did not stop. The record did.
What I write is emissions were rising until 2019, which says only what I know.
The second word is caused.
Depletion accelerated after 2015 and a new well opened in 2015.
Somebody asks me every year whether the well caused it, and I cannot tell from these numbers.
Rainfall was also lower from 2016, so I put the rainfall series on the same page.
By the time my sentence reaches a summary, were rising has become rose, and after has become because.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. Why does the series end in 2019?
2. What does the speaker write instead of rose?
3. Name two rival explanations for the faster depletion.
4. What happens to the sentence by the time it reaches a summary?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 the station was moved. 2 were rising.
3 consumption may have risen anyway; rainfall was lower from 2016.
4 were rising becomes rose, and after becomes because.
speaking.tutor: Retell the two carefully chosen words and ask the tutor which loss matters more.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Build a chain, then test it
speaking.instructions:
Build a causal chain of four steps about something you know, real or invented.
Use which in turn once and thereby once.
A model:
Consumption rose faster than recharge, depleting the aquifer, which in turn
lowered the water table, thereby drying out the habitat downstream.
Then say how many separate claims your chain contains, and which link is weakest.
Tap the mic. Say your chain and then your verdict on it.
Tap again and listen.
Check: after thereby, did you use an -ing form?
Could you describe the mechanism at every link, or only at some?
speaking.tutor: Say your chain to the tutor and ask which link it would challenge first.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: present the figures
speaking.instructions:
Present a set of figures for two minutes, real or invented.
Cover these five, in this order:
what was being measured, and what was not
what the trend was, and where the record stops
what is correlated, and what you are NOT claiming from it
what is projected, and on what assumption
what will be happening by the end of the projection period
Use at least three hedges from group 5 and at least one chain connective.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you state the assumption behind your projection?
Did you say caused anywhere you could not describe a mechanism?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your presentation and ask where you overstated the data.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Six sentences about a year from now
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about a project or a place a year from now.
Four must use the future continuous, for something already under way.
Two must use a plain future, for something that starts at that point.
Label each one UNDER WAY or STARTS.
writing.model:
By March we will be operating from two sites. (UNDER WAY)
This time next year the station will be measuring four pollutants. (UNDER WAY)
By 2031 the site will be working to the revised limit. (UNDER WAY)
In twelve months I will be finishing the second year of the course. (UNDER WAY)
The new limit will come into force in April. (STARTS)
We will move the station in September. (STARTS)
writing.criteria:
Four future continuous, each with will be plus an -ing form.
Two plain futures, each naming a starting point.
Every one correctly labelled.
No be dropped anywhere.
writing.support: Ask of each: at that moment, will it already be going on, or will it be beginning?
writing.extension: Turn one of your UNDER WAY sentences into a question about somebody's plans.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A data section
writing.prompt:
Write the Data and Trend sections of a monitoring summary, about 80 words.
Use the past continuous passive at least twice, for what was and was not
being measured.
Use the past continuous active at least once, for a figure that was moving.
Say where a record stops, and use the right tense for it.
Invent the subject.
writing.model:
1. Data. Water levels were being recorded at all four sites from 2010.
Only two pollutants were being measured before 2015; four are measured now.
The 2019 series ends at site 3, where the station was relocated.
2. Trend. Consumption was rising steadily until 2019. It appears to have levelled since.
Depletion accelerated after 2015.
writing.length: Two short sections, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
Two or more past continuous passives, describing what was being measured.
One or more past continuous actives, describing a moving figure.
Where a record stops, the continuous is used rather than the past simple.
At least one hedge from group 5.
writing.support: Write two lists first: what was measured, and what the figures did. Then choose the tense for each.
writing.extension: Write the sentence a summary would produce from yours, with the hedges removed, and say what was lost.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Four projections, with their assumptions
writing.prompt:
Write four projections about something you invent.
Use is expected to, is projected to, is likely to and is due to, one each.
Every one must state its assumption, in the same sentence or the next.
Then write one line saying what question all four leave unanswered.
writing.model:
Consumption is expected to fall by 2030, though no source for that expectation is given.
Depletion is projected to accelerate, assuming rainfall stays at the recent average.
The threshold is likely to be crossed by 2040 on current trends.
The replacement station is due to open in April, according to the published programme.

All four are passive, so none of them says WHO expects, projects or forecasts.
writing.criteria:
All four forms used, one each, followed by to plus a plain verb.
Every projection carries a stated assumption or basis.
is due to used for something scheduled, not for something calculated.
The closing line names the by-whom question.
writing.support: Write the assumption first. Then write the projection it supports.
writing.extension: Take the weakest of your four and write the sentence you would need before you could strengthen it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A chain, and an honest refusal
writing.prompt:
Part one. Write a causal chain of four steps about an invented situation,
using which in turn and thereby.
Part two. Write four sentences beneath it, one per link, saying whether you
could describe the mechanism for that link.
Part three. Write a paragraph about two things that are correlated in your
situation, stating clearly what you are NOT claiming from it.
writing.model:
Consumption rose faster than recharge, depleting the aquifer, which in turn
lowered the water table, thereby drying out the habitat downstream.

Link 1: yes. More taken out than put back reduces the store.
Link 2: yes. A smaller store means a lower table.
Link 3: yes, though the lag is unknown.
Link 4: only partly. Habitat drying has other causes, including rainfall.

Depletion accelerated after 2015 and a new well opened in 2015. The two are
correlated. I am not claiming the well caused it: consumption may have risen
anyway, and rainfall was also lower from 2016. These figures do not separate
the three.
writing.criteria:
which in turn followed by a full verb; thereby followed by an -ing form.
Four links, each judged separately.
At least one link honestly marked as unproved.
The final paragraph names at least two rival explanations.
writing.support: Build the chain first without hedges. Then test each link and add the hedges where they are needed.
writing.extension: Rewrite your chain so that a reader who rejects link 4 still accepts the first three.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Under way, or starting?
activities.instructions:
Choose the future continuous or the plain future.
1. The new system ___ (run) by this time next year. (already going)
2. The new limit ___ (come) into force in April. (it starts then)
3. By March they ___ (operate) from two sites. (already going)
4. We ___ (move) the station in September. (that is when it happens)
5. The station ___ (measure) four pollutants from April. (already going)
6. ___ you ___ (come) to the meeting? (their plans, not a commitment)
Now correct these.
7. This time next year we will using the new system.
8. I will be knowing the results by then.
activities.answers:
1. will be running  2. will come  3. will be operating  4. will move
5. will be measuring  6. Will you be coming
7. will BE using  8. I will know the results by then (know is a state verb)
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Ask of each one: at that moment, is it already going on, or is it beginning?

activities.title: Practice 2 — Moving, or finished?
activities.instructions:
Choose the past simple or the past continuous, active or passive.
1. Emissions ___ (rise) steadily until 2019, where the data ends.
2. Emissions ___ (rise) by four per cent in 2019.
3. Only two pollutants ___ (measure, passive) at that time.
4. The habitat ___ (survey, passive) when the work stopped.
5. Water levels ___ (not record, passive) before 2015.
6. Consumption ___ (fall) in the north and ___ (rise) in the south.
7. The station ___ (relocate, passive) in 2019.
Now write one sentence saying the trend was real and the data was partial.
activities.answers:
1. were rising  2. rose  3. were being measured  4. was being surveyed
5. were not being recorded  6. was falling / rising  7. was relocated
8. Emissions were rising, but only two pollutants were being measured.
Number 7 is a single finished event, so it takes the simple passive.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, ask whether the thing finished or the record finished.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Which projection?
activities.instructions:
Choose is expected to, is projected to, is likely to or is due to.
1. A calculation from present data shows depletion getting faster.
2. A timetable says the station opens in April.
3. It is probable but not certain that consumption will fall.
4. Everybody anticipates a fall, though nobody is named.
5. The published programme says the limit changes in 2031.
Now add the missing assumption.
6. Consumption is projected to fall by 2030.
7. The threshold will be crossed by 2040.
Now answer.
8. What question do all four forms leave unanswered?
activities.answers:
1. is projected to accelerate  2. is due to open  3. is likely to fall
4. is expected to fall  5. is due to change
6. ... assuming rainfall stays at the recent average.
7. On current trends, the threshold will be crossed by 2040.
8. By whom? All are passive, so none names who is projecting.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the basis beside each one first: a calculation, a timetable, or nothing stated.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Build the chain
activities.instructions:
Join each set into one chain.
1. Warmer water holds less oxygen. Fish numbers fall. (which in turn)
2. The store was enlarged. Pressure on the aquifer fell. (thereby)
3. Rainfall fell. Recharge was lower. The dry season was longer. (resulting in)
4. Consumption rose. The aquifer was depleted. The water table fell.
   The habitat dried out. (one four-step chain)
Now correct these.
5. The store was enlarged, thereby reduced pressure on the aquifer.
6. Warmer water holds less oxygen, which in turn reducing fish numbers.
Now answer.
7. How many separate claims does your answer to 4 contain?
activities.answers:
1. Warmer water holds less oxygen, which in turn reduces fish numbers.
2. The store was enlarged, thereby reducing pressure on the aquifer.
3. Rainfall fell, resulting in lower recharge and a longer dry season.
4. Consumption rose faster than recharge, depleting the aquifer, which in turn
   lowered the water table, thereby drying out the habitat downstream.
5. thereby REDUCING.  6. which in turn REDUCES.
7. Four. thereby takes -ing; which in turn takes a full verb.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the four steps as separate sentences first, then join them one link at a time.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Cause, or only correlation?
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each at the strength the evidence supports.
1. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July, so ice cream causes drowning.
2. Emissions rose and biodiversity fell, so emissions destroyed the habitat.
3. Transport is about a quarter of the total, so transport causes the problem.
4. Depletion accelerated after 2015 and the new well opened in 2015.
5. The new store opened and the shortage eased, so the store solved it.
Now answer.
6. Name the four ways two things that move together may be related.
7. What is the test before writing causes?
activities.answers:
1. They are correlated; both are probably driven by warm weather.
2. Emissions rose and biodiversity fell over the same period. A causal link
   would need a mechanism these figures do not give.
3. Transport contributes about a quarter of the total.
4. Depletion accelerated after the well opened, though the figures do not
   establish that the well caused it.
5. The shortage eased after the store opened. The store may have contributed.
6. A causes B; B causes A; something else causes both; coincidence.
7. Can you say HOW? If not, it is a correlation.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write the third possible cause before you rewrite it.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Put the hedge back
activities.instructions:
Each sentence has had its hedge removed, as happens when a figure travels.
Rewrite it so it says only what the evidence supports.
1. Emissions rose until 2019. (the series ends there; the line is still going up)
2. Depletion accelerated because the well opened. (you have no mechanism)
3. Consumption will fall by 2030. (it is a projection, on an assumption)
4. Biodiversity is unchanged. (it is, except at one site)
5. Consumption is forty-one thousand two hundred litres. (it is an estimate)
6. These are the figures for site 3. (they may be revised)
activities.answers:
1. Emissions were rising until 2019, where the series ends.
2. Depletion accelerated after the well opened.
3. Consumption is projected to fall by 2030, assuming rainfall stays at the recent average.
4. Biodiversity is broadly unchanged, with one site declining.
5. Consumption is estimated at approximately forty thousand litres.
6. Figures for site 3 are tentative and may be revised.
In 5, note that approximately should not sit in front of a precise number.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write what you actually know, then write the sentence that says exactly that.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the summary
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. What is the baseline year?
2. Why does the 2019 series end at site 3?
3. What does the projection assume?
4. Copy two past continuous passives and say what each tells you.
5. Copy the sentence that refuses to claim a cause, and say what it refuses.
6. Copy the future continuous and say what it claims about 2031.
activities.answers:
1. 2010.
2. The station was relocated, so later readings are not comparable.
3. That rainfall remains at the 2016 to 2024 average.
4. 'Water levels were being recorded at all four sites from 2010' and 'Only two
   pollutants were being measured before 2015.' Each says what the arrangement
   was over a period, not on one occasion.
5. 'These figures do not establish which, if either, is responsible.' It refuses
   to turn a shared year into a cause.
6. 'By 2031 the site will be operating under the revised abstraction limit.'
   It claims the limit will already be in force and running by then.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the summary with a pen and mark every hedge before you answer.

quizzes.q: This time next year we ___ the new system.
quizzes.why: will is always followed by a plain verb, and here that plain verb is be. Dropping the be is the commonest error with this form.

quizzes.q: Which asks about somebody's plans rather than asking them to commit?
options: Will you come to the meeting?
Will you be coming to the meeting?
Do you come to the meeting?
Are you coming to the meeting or not?
quizzes.a: Will you be coming to the meeting?
quizzes.why: The continuous removes the sense of a request, which is why it is the politer of the two.

quizzes.q: The series ends in 2019 and the line is still going up. Emissions ___ until 2019.
quizzes.why: The movement did not stop in 2019; the record did. The past simple would claim a finished movement the data does not show.

quizzes.q: Only two pollutants ___ at that time.
quizzes.why: It describes the arrangement over a period, not a single occasion. were measured would suggest one act of measuring.

quizzes.q: A calculation from present data shows depletion getting faster. Depletion ___ accelerate.
quizzes.why: projected means calculated from present data. is due to is for something scheduled by a timetable.

quizzes.q: What question do 'is expected to' and 'is projected to' both leave unanswered?
quizzes.why: Both are passive, so neither names who is expecting or projecting. It is the by-whom question from Unit 4, in a new place.

quizzes.q: The store was enlarged, thereby ___ pressure on the aquifer.
quizzes.why: thereby takes an -ing form. which in turn is the one that takes a full verb: which in turn reduced it.

quizzes.q: Warmer water holds less oxygen, ___ reduces fish numbers.
quizzes.why: reduces is a full verb, so it needs which in turn. thereby and resulting in both require an -ing form.

quizzes.q: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July. What follows?
options: They are correlated, probably through warm weather.
quizzes.a: They are correlated, probably through warm weather.
quizzes.why: When two things move together there are four possibilities, and something else causing both is the commonest.

quizzes.q: What is the test before writing that X causes Y?
quizzes.why: If you can name a mechanism you may have a cause. If you cannot, you have a correlation, and there is a word for that.

quizzes.q: Transport is about a quarter of the total. The honest verb is:
quizzes.why: contributes says one of several causes, which is what a quarter of a total supports. The other three each claim the whole mechanism.

options: Consumption is estimated at approximately 40,000 litres.
quizzes.a: Consumption is estimated at approximately 40,000 litres.
quizzes.why: estimate takes at, and approximately should not stand in front of a precise figure: approximately 41,237 claims accuracy it then withdraws.

teacherNotes.note: The future continuous (9Ug.09) is the last new verb form in the course and appears nowhere below this unit. Everything else increments: the past continuous from five earlier cards, the future passive from Unit 10, and connectives from Units 6, 7 and 13.

The plan's patterns here were hedging, cause and correlation, and citing a source. The first two are cards 5 and 3; citing a source belongs to 9Us.02 and is taught in Unit 18. What the plan omitted is the future continuous, which 9Ug.09 names explicitly and which is placed only here.

'will using' without the be is the same error as 'must signed' in Unit 10 and 'has withdrawn' in the same unit: a modal or auxiliary followed by a plain verb, with the plain verb dropped. Point at the pattern across the three units rather than treating it as new.
thereby takes -ing and which in turn takes a full verb. Learners mix them freely because both mean roughly 'and so'. Practice 4 items 5 and 6 are the same error in both directions.

Card 5 teaches restraint about causation, and it would be easy for a class to conclude that nothing can ever be claimed. The card gives an honest middle — contributes to, appears to have caused, may account for part of — and says that is where most real writing sits. Reading 1 models the same balance: the writer refuses a causal claim and still publishes the rainfall series so a reader can weigh it.

Group 5 is deliberately mild. Unit 6 taught admittedly and arguably for arguments; these five hedge FIGURES, which is a different job. approximately in front of a precise number (approximately 41,237) is the error worth naming, because it withdraws the accuracy it just claimed.

Practice 6 is the unit's real assessment: six sentences with their hedges stripped out, to be restored. It mirrors the reading's observation that hedges are what disappear first when a figure travels, which makes it a test of judgement rather than of vocabulary.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I will be doing at a point next year.
I never drop the be from will be.
I know that 'were rising' and 'rose' claim different things.
I can say what was being measured over a period.
I state the assumption behind every projection I write.
I know that thereby takes -ing and which in turn takes a full verb.
I ask whether I can describe HOW before I write that X causes Y.
I can spot a hedge that has been removed from somebody else's sentence.

assignment.title: The summary, and what a shorter version would lose
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write a monitoring summary for something you invent, in five sections
and about 170 words: Data, Trend, Thresholds, Projection, Note.
Data must use the past continuous passive at least twice.
Trend must use the past continuous for at least one figure whose record stops.
Projection must use two of the projection forms and state its assumption.
It must also contain one future continuous sentence about the end of the period.
Part two. Somewhere in your summary, two things are correlated. Write a paragraph
naming them, giving at least two rival explanations, and saying what you are not claiming.
Part three. Now write the three-sentence version a summary would produce from yours,
with the hedges removed. Then write four lines naming exactly what was lost, and
whether any of the losses was dishonest.
Part four. Build one four-step causal chain from your own figures, and judge each
link separately: can you describe the mechanism, or not?
